blocks.prompt: 2 (i) Use the remainder theorem to find the remainder when the first polynomial is divided by the second polynomial: \(x^{2} + 5x + 6\), \(x - 2\).
blocks.explanation:
The question names the method: the remainder theorem, so no long division is needed.
We must find the remainder when \(x^{2} + 5x + 6\) is divided by \(x - 2\).
Plan: write the divisor as \(x - a\), then the remainder is simply \(f(a)\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{2} + 5x + 6\), divisor \(x - 2\).
To find: the remainder.
Method: Remainder theorem: if \(f(x)\) is divided by \(x - a\), the remainder is \(f(a)\). It saves us the long division.

Write the divisor as \(x - a\)
\[x - 2 = x - a\]
\[a = 2\]
Why: The remainder theorem is stated for a divisor of the form \(x - a\).

Put \(x = 2\) in \(f(x)\)
\[f(2) = (2)^{2} + 5(2) + 6\]
\[= 4 + 10 + 6\]
\[= 20\]
Why: Work out each power first, then multiply by the coefficient.

Read the remainder
\[R = f(2) = 20\]
Why: By the remainder theorem the value \(f(2)\) is the remainder.

Check: synthetic division by \(x - 2\)
\[\begin{array}{r|rrr} 2 & 1 & 5 & 6 \\  &  & 2 & 14 \\ \hline & 1 & 7 & \boxed{20} \end{array}\]
Why: The last number of the bottom row is the remainder; it is \(20\), the same as \(f(2)\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (ii) Use the remainder theorem to find the remainder when the first polynomial is divided by the second polynomial: \(x^{3} + 5x^{2} + 6\), \(x + 1\).
blocks.explanation:
The question names the method: the remainder theorem, so no long division is needed.
We must find the remainder when \(x^{3} + 5x^{2} + 6\) is divided by \(x + 1\).
Plan: write the divisor as \(x - a\), then the remainder is simply \(f(a)\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{3} + 5x^{2} + 6\), divisor \(x + 1\).
To find: the remainder.
Method: Remainder theorem: if \(f(x)\) is divided by \(x - a\), the remainder is \(f(a)\). It saves us the long division.

Write the divisor as \(x - a\)
\[x + 1 = x - (-1)\]
\[a = -1\]
Why: The theorem needs the form \(x - a\); a plus sign in the divisor means \(a\) is negative.

Put \(x = -1\) in \(f(x)\)
\[f(-1) = (-1)^{3} + 5(-1)^{2} + 6\]
\[= -1 + 5 + 6\]
\[= 10\]
Why: An even power of a negative number is positive and an odd power is negative.

Read the remainder
\[R = f(-1) = 10\]
Why: By the remainder theorem the value \(f(-1)\) is the remainder.

Check: synthetic division by \(x + 1\)
\[\begin{array}{r|rrrr} -1 & 1 & 5 & 0 & 6 \\  &  & -1 & -4 & 4 \\ \hline & 1 & 4 & -4 & \boxed{10} \end{array}\]
Why: The last number of the bottom row is the remainder; it is \(10\), the same as \(f(-1)\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (iii) Use the remainder theorem to find the remainder when the first polynomial is divided by the second polynomial: \(x^{4} + x^{3} + x^{2} + x + 1\), \(x - 1\).
blocks.explanation:
The question names the method: the remainder theorem, so no long division is needed.
We must find the remainder when \(x^{4} + x^{3} + x^{2} + x + 1\) is divided by \(x - 1\).
Plan: write the divisor as \(x - a\), then the remainder is simply \(f(a)\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{4} + x^{3} + x^{2} + x + 1\), divisor \(x - 1\).
To find: the remainder.
Method: Remainder theorem: if \(f(x)\) is divided by \(x - a\), the remainder is \(f(a)\). It saves us the long division.

Write the divisor as \(x - a\)
\[x - 1 = x - a\]
\[a = 1\]
Why: The remainder theorem is stated for a divisor of the form \(x - a\).

Read the remainder
\[R = f(1) = 5\]
Why: By the remainder theorem the value \(f(1)\) is the remainder.

Check: synthetic division by \(x - 1\)
\[\begin{array}{r|rrrrr} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\  &  & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & \boxed{5} \end{array}\]
Why: The last number of the bottom row is the remainder; it is \(5\), the same as \(f(1)\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (iv) Use the remainder theorem to find the remainder when the first polynomial is divided by the second polynomial: \(x^{4} + x^{2} + 1\), \(x + 3\).
blocks.explanation:
The question names the method: the remainder theorem, so no long division is needed.
We must find the remainder when \(x^{4} + x^{2} + 1\) is divided by \(x + 3\).
Plan: write the divisor as \(x - a\), then the remainder is simply \(f(a)\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{4} + x^{2} + 1\), divisor \(x + 3\).
To find: the remainder.
Method: Remainder theorem: if \(f(x)\) is divided by \(x - a\), the remainder is \(f(a)\). It saves us the long division.

Write the divisor as \(x - a\)
\[x + 3 = x - (-3)\]
\[a = -3\]
Why: The theorem needs the form \(x - a\); a plus sign in the divisor means \(a\) is negative.

Put \(x = -3\) in \(f(x)\)
\[f(-3) = (-3)^{4} + (-3)^{2} + 1\]
\[= 81 + 9 + 1\]
\[= 91\]
Why: An even power of a negative number is positive and an odd power is negative.

Read the remainder
\[R = f(-3) = 91\]
Why: By the remainder theorem the value \(f(-3)\) is the remainder.

Check: synthetic division by \(x + 3\)
\[\begin{array}{r|rrrrr} -3 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\  &  & -3 & 9 & -30 & 90 \\ \hline & 1 & -3 & 10 & -30 & \boxed{91} \end{array}\]
Why: The last number of the bottom row is the remainder; it is \(91\), the same as \(f(-3)\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (v) Use the remainder theorem to find the remainder when the first polynomial is divided by the second polynomial: \(x^{4} + x^{3} + 2\), \(x + 2\).
blocks.explanation:
The question names the method: the remainder theorem, so no long division is needed.
We must find the remainder when \(x^{4} + x^{3} + 2\) is divided by \(x + 2\).
Plan: write the divisor as \(x - a\), then the remainder is simply \(f(a)\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{4} + x^{3} + 2\), divisor \(x + 2\).
To find: the remainder.
Method: Remainder theorem: if \(f(x)\) is divided by \(x - a\), the remainder is \(f(a)\). It saves us the long division.

Write the divisor as \(x - a\)
\[x + 2 = x - (-2)\]
\[a = -2\]
Why: The theorem needs the form \(x - a\); a plus sign in the divisor means \(a\) is negative.

Put \(x = -2\) in \(f(x)\)
\[f(-2) = (-2)^{4} + (-2)^{3} + 2\]
\[= 16 - 8 + 2\]
\[= 10\]
Why: An even power of a negative number is positive and an odd power is negative.

Read the remainder
\[R = f(-2) = 10\]
Why: By the remainder theorem the value \(f(-2)\) is the remainder.

Check: synthetic division by \(x + 2\)
\[\begin{array}{r|rrrrr} -2 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\  &  & -2 & 2 & -4 & 8 \\ \hline & 1 & -1 & 2 & -4 & \boxed{10} \end{array}\]
Why: The last number of the bottom row is the remainder; it is \(10\), the same as \(f(-2)\).
